title: Onigiri
subtitle: Japanese rice balls with tuna mayo filling
excerpt: Onigiri are Japanese rice balls shaped by hand into triangles and filled with a small amount of savoury filling. They are Japan's most popular portable snack. Short-grain rice is the key -- it holds together where long-grain falls apart.
sourceNotes: Onigiri are Japanese rice balls, eaten as a snack or packed lunch since at least the Heian period (794--1185). They are mentioned in Lady Murasaki's diary from around 1000 AD. Modern convenience store onigiri, wrapped in plastic that keeps the nori crisp until opened, were introduced in 1978.

content.text: Onigiri are straightforward once you have the right rice. Short-grain Japanese rice is starchy enough to hold its shape when pressed. Long-grain or basmati rice will not bind. The shaping technique takes a couple of tries to get right -- the rice should be warm, your hands should be cold and wet, and you press firmly.

items.prepNote: use Japanese short-grain rice -- rinse until water runs clear, cook with slightly less water than usual
for shaping -- wet your hands and press salt onto palms
use soy sauce -- for a dipping option alongside
use canned tuna in oil for filling -- drain and mix with a little mayonnaise

content.text: Cook the rice and let it cool slightly until you can handle it -- it should still be warm.
Wet your hands with cold water. Sprinkle a little salt on your palms. This stops sticking and seasons the rice.
Place a generous handful of rice in one palm. Press a small indent in the centre and add a teaspoon of tuna filling.
Close the rice around the filling. Shape into a triangle by pressing firmly with both hands, turning and reshaping with each press. Aim for a firm, compact triangle about 7cm across.
Leave plain, or wrap a strip of dried nori around the base. Serve with soy sauce for dipping.

items.cause: Rice too dry or not pressed firmly enough
items.fix: Use short-grain Japanese rice -- it has more starch and holds together much better than basmati or long-grain. Press firmly and evenly when shaping.

content.text: Onigiri are Japan's ultimate portable food. They are sold in every convenience store across the country, with rotating seasonal fillings. Common fillings include pickled plum (umeboshi), salmon, and tuna mayo. They are eaten at picnics, school lunches, and late-night snacks.
